conclusion: Complete unchecked-hash bytecode halves the cold imports phase on every CPU part Lambda gave us (CPU part 0xd40 as read from /proc/cpuinfo, n=49/52: 0.719 -> 0.346 s, delta -0.373 s, 95% CI [-0.380, -0.367]; 0xd0c and 0xd4f have sparse same-direction observations (an opposite sparse sign would make the result host-conditioned); all 12 shared cells below 0, with 5 sparse unmatched cells reported separately) and Init Duration by -0.380 s on 0xd40. Mechanism confirmed in-function: ctl recompiles all 153-157 task-root modules from source in every environment (0 usable .pyc), pyc recompiles 1 (the e6_entry wrapper itself). The cold first request does NOT improve: on 0xd40 first_request_total delta -0.012 s, CI [-0.098, +0.079]. On 0xd0c (n=5/3 only) it is -0.685 s, CI [-1.168, -0.322]; on 0xd4f (n=6/5) +0.047 s, CI [-0.271, +0.250]. That is no consistent improvement across parts. The reason: the on-demand load runs in PR #77's background thread and the request waits for the ~25 s S3 download, which starts after imports either way; the saved ~0.37 s goes back into wait_for_load (weight_download on pyc +0.30 s, CI [+0.258, +0.383], a download that starts earlier and ends at the same time: import_total + weight_download p50 25.75 vs 25.68 s). Billed cold duration is unchanged (REPORT Billed Duration includes Init; the Init saved is spent waiting for the load inside Duration). SnapStart snapshot init imports also halve on both CPU parts Lambda prepared snapshots on, each record bound to the CPU part in its own log stream (0xd40 0.660 -> 0.326 s, n=3/3; 0xd0c 0.838 -> 0.408 s, n=3/3; every delta beyond the control spread across published versions; 12/12 records linked, 0 missing, 0 ambiguous), but that is publish time, not restore latency: restore first request total delta -0.045 s, CI [-0.097, +0.014] (0xd40 only). Warm inference unchanged (+0.0077 s, CI [-0.0100, +0.0251]). Answers: 420/420 pyc answers bit-identical to ctl for the same request and CPU part, and every answer P1's reference covers is bit-identical to it. Recommendation: adopt (no cost, +7 MB zip / +19 MB unzipped of the 250 MB limit, ~9 MB less peak memory) as hygiene; it pays off only where imports are on the request path, i.e. after a change that overlaps or removes the download (E4, E5, E9 or a combined ladder rung), so R should re-measure it there rather than credit it to the current baseline.

assessment.deployment_headlines: no consistent cold-first-request, restore, or warm benefit across observed CPU parts and rounds

primary_effect.reason: every assessed cell has a negative delta whose absolute size exceeds its control within-cell spread; sparse cells and CPU parts are unassessed and have no opposite observed sign

assessment.rerun: not needed: host-adjusted assessed cells support one imports-phase outcome; sparse CPU parts and unmatched cells remain explicit limitations, while deployment headlines remain null

host_variability.method: Within each observed CPU part, compare arm medians in each round. Arms are sequential waves whose first position alternates by round; this is alternation, not within-round interleaving. A directional effect must exceed the control observations' within-cell range in every assessed shared cell; deltas inside that range support a null outcome even if their signs vary. Every shared cell persists its own outcome (within-control-variation, negative- or positive-beyond-control-variation, or unassessed), and each CPU part's outcome is aggregated from those persisted cell outcomes. A cell with fewer than two control observations has no spread estimate and is explicitly unassessed, but its observed sign is kept: an opposite sign on an unassessed cell makes its CPU part host-conditioned even when the part's assessed cells agree, and an opposite sign on a wholly unassessed part blocks a comparable directional outcome. Missing-arm cells and rows without CPU identity are listed but never treated as comparable strata.

assessment.reason: every assessed CPU part has the same outcome against its control spread across published versions; sparse CPU parts have no opposite-sign observation; missing, ambiguous and unpublished records are excluded and counted

limits: snapshot inits run inside publish_version, so this is publish time, not a request-path latency

only the CPU part is observable for a snapshot init (the engine's init log line); variant, revision, HWCAP, features, CPU count and kernel come from e6_entry's first-invocation record, which a snapshot init does not emit, so they are unknown here
availability zone, physical host and cgroup limits are unknown
Lambda chose which CPU parts to prepare per version; one init per (version, part, arm), so spread is across versions, not within a version
no Graviton generation is inferred from the CPU part
snapshot_init.method: Each before_snapshot record is bound to the CPU part named by the `decider.engine init cpu_part=` line in its own log stream (one stream = one execution environment); binding never crosses streams. Only streams of versions this run published count. A stream with no known part is missing, one with more than one distinct part is ambiguous; neither is a comparison stratum. Within each CPU part, the pyc-minus-ctl median delta across published versions is judged against the range of ctl's per-version values (cell_outcome); a part with fewer than two control inits is unassessed, and an opposite observed sign on such a sparse part blocks a comparable directional outcome.

hypothesis: P1's function.zip ships no usable Python bytecode: 149 .pyc whose source-mtime headers do not match the 2026-01-01 stamp the build gives every .py, and no .pyc at all for most modules. /var/task is read-only, so every cold start (and every SnapStart snapshot init) compiles every imported module from source and cannot cache it. Shipping complete unchecked-hash bytecode cuts the cold `imports` phase, and therefore Init Duration and the start of the background model load, with no change to answers, warm inference or restore.
